newsitem.title: CHINA: China share offer seen aimed at deflecting Kodak.
newsitem.headline: China share offer seen aimed at deflecting Kodak.

text.p: China's biggest domestic producer of film plans to offer shares to the public in a bid to elude American suitor and competitor, Eastman Kodak Co, analysts and industry officials said on Monday.

China Lucky Film Corp wants to offer A shares to domestic investors to raise cash to compete with the big U.S. company, which has long sought control of Lucky as part of a deal that would give it a commanding share of the growing China market.
"We need funds to expand our market share," said Lucky Film official Zhou Jicai.
"The door is still open to Kodak but any decision (on cooperation) would be made on the basis of whether it is in the national interest."

China's official media said on Sunday that state-run Lucky was hoping to offer stock to the public to boost sales of its photographic film, which have lost ground due to competition from foreign manufacturers such as Kodak and Japan's Fuji Photo Film Co.
Lucky officials did not say how many shares would be offered or how much money would be raised.
"We still need approval for this from securities regulators," Zhou told Reuters by telephone from the company's headquarters in the northern city of Baoding.
Industry officials said that Kodak has long been discussing a package deal that would allow it to take over several struggling Chinese film producers in return for the chance to buy control of Lucky.
Neither Kodak nor Fuji manufactures film in China, and the American giant has been eager to ensure a stronger foothold in the market by manufacturing locally.

Kodak and Fuji have set up developing shops across China in a move that sharply eroded Lucky's market share. Lucky is preparing to open 1,000 such franchise stores nationwide, the Business Weekly said on Sunday.
Lucky's share of the domestic market is about 20 percent, according to Chinese estimates.
It has been willing to cooperate with Kodak but not at the cost of giving up control of the company or eliminating its brand from the market.
Kodak was unlikely to accept a minority stake in any venture with Lucky, an industry analyst said.
He also said the proposed stock offer appeared to make cooperation between the two companies less likely.
An industry official said the issue was politically sensitive and unlikely to be resolved soon.
"There are two schools of thought within the government," said an official at the Ministry of Chemicals Industry, which oversees Lucky and has been involved in negotiations with Kodak.
"One is to allow a takeover as the industry is not strategic while the other is to protect a company which has a recognised brand," the official told Reuters.
Lucky would be able to use the badly need funds raised from a share issue to compete with its rivals.
But if the talks continued with Kodak, the funds would also strengthen Lucky's position at the bargaining table, the official said.

Jessica Chan, Kodak's assistant public relations manager in Hong Kong, declined to comment on Lucky's strategy but she said the U.S. company had been discussing plans for the China market with central, provincial and local governments as well as state enterprises.
"There are a number of enterprises and Lucky is one of them," she said. "The discussions are still continuing."
